introduction.p: The derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives. Multiplication by a constant also passes through differentiation. We will prove these rules from the limit definition and use them to differentiate polynomials.

exercise.title: Why do added constants disappear under differentiation?

statement.p: The graphs of x^2 and x^2+5 have the same tangent slopes. In your own words, why does the derivative record change and therefore forget vertical shifts?

hint.p: A vertical shift does not change rise over run. The sum rule together with (C)'=0 is the algebraic form of that sentence.

statement.p: The rate of change of a sum is the sum of the rates, and local linear approximations add the way ordinary lines add. In your own words, why do those two statements belong together, and why do they still not handle a product?

hint.p: If two quantities change independently, their total change is the sum of the two changes. A product has an interaction: each factor helps change the product.

subsection.title: Derivatives of polynomials
subsection.p: A polynomial is built from powers of x, constants, constant multiples, and sums. The rules above therefore give the derivative of every polynomial.

A product changes in a different way from a sum. If one side of a rectangle changes, the area changes. If both sides change, the area changes for two reasons at once.
That is where the product rule comes from.

exercise.title: Why are sum and scaling not enough?

statement.p: Linearity differentiates every polynomial, but not every useful function is a polynomial. In your own words, why does expanding a product fail as a general strategy, and what new kind of change does a product introduce?

hint.p: Expansion is unpleasant or impossible for many products. If both sides of a rectangle change, the area changes for two reasons at once.
